Our method improves the quality of various sparse-view Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed, and our analysis works on different prior models. Project page: https://linwk20.github.io/spectral-fusion-gs/

articles.title: Byte Patches versus BPE at Matched Data: A Matched-Twin Comparison at 350M Parameters
articles.summary: We compare a MEGABYTE-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder (local64) to a matched byte-level 8k BPE decoder (BPE-8k) under identical raw bytes, document order, and approximately matched bytes per optimizer step: 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. Under matched-span document sliding (identical scored byte ranges), BPE-8k leads with relative gaps of -5.2%, -4.9%, -9.3% and -6.1% in bits per byte (overall, text, code, math; paired bootstrap). Downstream, CharBench equal fine-tuning favors local64 (53.7% vs 40.0%), fact200 favors BPE-8k (16.5% vs 7.0%), and PIQA (raw and length-normalized) and ARC-Easy length-normalized favor BPE-8k after Holm correction at alpha = 0.05; remaining tasks are ties. Evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions include context-length extrapolation past the BPE training context, bits per token reported as bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators. Unlike controlled tokenizer studies that vary the subword tokenizer under a fixed token budget, or FLOP-controlled byte-model scaling studies, we hold the raw bytes, their order and the optimizer recipe fixed and ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can replace the tokenizer at all. Limits: one size, one seed, one 8k vocabulary fixed before the runs, and a known difference in embedding initialization between the twins.

articles.title: Mind the Band: The Hidden Frequency Variable in Geometric RoPE
articles.summary: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) incorporate 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies--its frequency band--yet existing implementations leave this band to inherited defaults, either retaining standard 2D RoPE's top frequency or letting the frequency span grow exponentially with the attention head dimension. We show that this unstandardized setting can reverse benchmark rankings. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline in the 47M model (144-channel heads), yet trails by 1.2 dB in the 25M model (48-channel heads), and exhibits the same reversal when varying head size alone at fixed model width. Populating a 243x range with four frequencies instead of the 3x default at 48 channels recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. Across view synthesis and two-view depth estimation, overly narrow bands consistently blur correspondence, whereas all three projection-based encodings perform reliably when their top frequency lies within 0.3--3 rotations per 8-pixel patch (10--90 rotations across 256x256 RealEstate10K). At the opposite extreme, overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE through a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass, yet leaves their gradients with respect to predicted depth undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90--93% of the lost PSNR, showing that forward smoothing does not guarantee backward stability. Guided by this analysis, we distill practical guidelines--setting bands in image coordinates, populating spans in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping--and advocate reporting and matching frequency bands in future multi-view benchmarks.

articles.title: Best Arm Identification with Unknown Post-Action Context Distribution
articles.summary: We study best arm identification (BAI) with post-action context in the fixed-confidence setting. After choosing an action, the learner observes a post-action context together with a reward whose distribution depends only on this context. Incorporating such intermediate information can substantially reduce the sample complexity of identifying the best arm. While Shahverdikondori et al. (2026a) analyzed the case where the distribution of contexts given actions is known, we address the more challenging and practically relevant case where this distribution is unknown. We derive an instance-dependent sample complexity lower bound and propose a Track-and-Stop algorithm that matches it asymptotically with access to an optimization oracle. Our stopping rule uses a new concentration inequality that jointly controls uncertainty in the context distributions and reward means, removing the factor of two incurred by separate concentration bounds. Implementing the algorithm generally requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. We propose a convex relaxation with instance-dependent approximation guarantees, including asymptotic tightness on hard Gaussian instances. Experiments demonstrate that exploiting post-action context reduces the sample complexity relative to baselines that ignore it, even when the context distributions are unknown.

articles.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
articles.summary: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.

articles.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
articles.summary: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

articles.title: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth
articles.summary: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

articles.title: How to build and train your recurrent-depth model: A fixed-point perspective
articles.summary: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.

articles.title: Metamorphic Testing of Learned Spatial Surrogates for Transit Accessibility
articles.summary: Transit-network design requires evaluating many candidates, but detailed accessibility calculations are too slow to repeat inside an optimization loop. We therefore train a neural surrogate to approximate them. Given a candidate bus network and fixed information about rail service and nearby opportunities, it predicts the calculated spatial change in accessibility. We compare its predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions and test specified qualitative relations under controlled input changes. Reference calculations on constructed networks assess the applicability of relations that have a routing-level counterpart. Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests. One targeted intervention substantially increases pass rates for two connectivity relations while predictive skill also improves. Average prediction error is therefore insufficient when a learned model becomes an optimization objective. Predictive agreement and controlled behavioral tests should be reported separately.

articles.title: BODYBENCH: Evaluating Adversarial Image Defenses Against AI Nudification Inpainting
articles.summary: Adversarial perturbation defenses protect images from unauthorized edits by adding imperceptible noise. Yet none of these methods have been evaluated against nudification, despite AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) being among the most documented harms of generative AI. Moreover, nudification edits are readily carried out through inpainting, the primary setting these protection methods are designed to defend against. We argue this is a problem-formulation failure since prior threat models do not correspond to nudification edits (also called attacks). The misalignment of existing approaches is structural, spanning mask shape, training and testing prompt distributions, and success criterion which causes existing evaluations to systematically overestimate protection effectiveness. We reformulate image protection against unauthorized editing around this documented harm. We introduce BODYBENCH, a benchmark of 648 fully synthetic clothed adult subjects, each paired with 11 mask variants spanning body, face, and context regions. We propose three harm-aligned metrics: sexualization, naturalness, and recognizability that jointly determine whether an inpainted output constitutes a successful nudification attack. Auditing four recent protection methods (PhotoGuard, DiffusionGuard, AdvPaint, DiffVax) on BODYBENCH, we find that protection succeeds in only one configuration of one method, and only under exact mask alignment between defender and attacker---a condition no real defender can guarantee and one that we show is easily always bypassed. We also show that standard evaluation metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) are essentially uncorrelated with nudification protection. BODYBENCH makes this misalignment measurable and provides a foundation for defenses grounded in documented harm.

articles.title: 零基础也能做开发，智元灵心平台一年孵化超3万个机器人智能体
One, No One and One Hundred Thousand CTs: Testing Anatomical Control in Text-to-CT Generation
articles.summary: Recent advances in deep learning and the public availability of computed tomography (CT) datasets with paired reports have enabled many Text-to-CT generators. However, their evaluations almost always differ in preprocessing and metrics, which hinders comparison. Moreover, their protocols almost never test how editing the report changes the CT, not even at the same seed, so the report is often assumed to control the anatomy without evidence of how much and how consistently it does. We therefore propose CtrlCT, a toolkit that tests two properties of a generator, Credibility and Control. Credibility tests compare generated CTs, as a population, with real CTs and reports; Control tests are metamorphic and need no reference CT: at a fixed seed, editing one finding should change it as requested, keep negated findings absent and shift distant anatomy no more than a new seed, and the change should hold across seeds. A Report Card summarises all measures and insights for each generator. We benchmark five public generators on 940 chest CTs and 687 edits of pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, holding out a sixth to test the toolkit. Among them, the most credible generators barely respond to an added effusion, while the most responsive produce less realistic and less diverse CTs. The analyses proposed in the literature do not reveal this. We release CtrlCT, its edits, seeds and 30,525 synthetic CTs after acceptance.

articles.title: Support2Sim: Visually Faithful Real2Sim with Stable Object Supports
articles.summary: Reconstructing a scene for physics simulation requires recovering its spatial layout and the support relationships that govern its behavior. We present Support2Sim, a Real2Sim system that reconstructs simulation-ready scenes from a single RGB image. Our design objective is to maximize source fidelity, support realization, and stability within a practical time budget for scene generation. Support2Sim infers a support graph, which a contact-guided pose initializer uses to propose poses for objects with multiple supports. The initializer generates and ranks candidates by geometric fit and source-image agreement. A coarse-to-fine refiner allocates a fixed search budget across supported objects and evaluates pose updates with physics rollouts. After an accepted update, it searches from the new pose at a finer translation and rotation scale. We benchmark our method on 50 scenes spanning four datasets. Compared with the strongest baseline, Support2Sim improves source-mask IoU after 10 seconds by 21.4 pp, realizes 87.1% versus 73.2% of intended supports, and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm. See our project page at https://support2sim.github.io for more details.

articles.title: Capability and Interpretability of Transformers on Multi-task Recurrence
articles.summary: Transformers are widely used in various language tasks, with limited understanding of their internal mechanisms. Motivated by the recurrent structure of many linguistic rules, we study the capability and interpretability of Transformers through a controlled family of linear recurrence tasks over finite cyclic groups. These tasks range from executing a single fixed rule to identifying a latent rule from context and switching between explicitly specified rules, with and without input masking. Through extensive experiments across different configurations, we find that switching specified rules is simpler than identifying latent rules for Transformers in general. We also identify how several key factors affect the generalization capability of Transformers, including the depth, width, and the algebraic structure of the linear recurrence. Curriculum training is extremely useful when the number of rules is large. With standard tools in mechanistic interpretability like linear probing and input patching, our study reveals how Transformers represent, identify, and execute multiple rules.

articles.title: DocPristine: Content-Aware Document Appearance Enhancement under Real-World Mixed Degradations
articles.summary: Camera-captured documents often exhibit mixed degradations, such as highlights, shadows, and blur, that distort backgrounds and obscure text details. Document appearance enhancement (DAE) aims to mitigate these degradations and improve readability. Existing document appearance enhancement methods rely either on input-derived visual cues that can become unreliable under severe degradation or on LLM-based degradation diagnosis that lacks spatial guidance. Notably, we find that pretrained document visual encoders continue to attend to text regions in degraded documents, providing content-aware guidance. Based on this insight, we propose DocPristine, which adaptively fuses multi-layer features from a frozen document visual encoder and injects them into a pixel restoration network. To integrate these features into a pixel restoration network, DocPristine combines Adaptive Multi-Layer Feature Fusion (AMFF), Hierarchical Gated Conditioning (HGC), and Shifted-Window Cross-Attention (SWCA). Specifically, SWCA draws on structural cues from neighboring locations across window boundaries to recover fine text details.We also introduce DocACE, with a synthetic mixed-degradation training set (DocACE-Synthetic) and a real-world test set (DocACE-Real) containing manually restored ground-truth images and document parsing annotations. Comprehensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that DocPristine achieves state-of-the-art appearance enhancement quality and consistently improves downstream document parsing. Code, models, and data will be publicly available.

articles.title: DiCT: Teaching X-ray Vision-Language Models to Reason via Imagining CT
articles.summary: Diagnosing with X-rays often requires reasoning about the 3D locations of abnormalities and their spatial relationships to surrounding anatomical structures, yet such reasoning remains challenging due to the loss of spatial information in 2D projections. To address this challenge, we propose Dreaming in CT (DiCT), a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that leverages a CT vision-language model (VLM) to guide an X-ray VLM. Through this CT-guided transfer, the student acquires CT-informed 3D reasoning capabilities, enabling it to reason directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference time. The framework begins with instruct the dreamer, which equips the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning capabilities and establishes a structured interface that distinguishes X-ray observations from CT imagination. Building on this structure, visualize the dream introduces CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD), where the CT teacher selectively guides the X-ray student's reasoning trajectories to transfer 3D anatomical knowledge. Finally, manifest the dream adapts the acquired reasoning capabilities from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. Experiments across two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA demonstrate DiCT's effectiveness across radiological reasoning tasks, achieving a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77$\times$ lower inference computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongYep/DiCT.

articles.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
articles.summary: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found at https://github.com/urbste/weight-space-programming-ptq

articles.title: HazeFlux: Few-Step Generative Priors for Real-World Image Dehazing
articles.summary: Real-world single-image dehazing suffers from severe domain shifts, as paired real data is scarce and models trained on synthetic haze generalize poorly to real-world haze. While pre-trained generative editing models offer powerful image priors to bridge this generalization gap, applying them to image dehazing poses two major challenges: standard generative models prioritize distribution alignment over strict pixel-level fidelity, and operating in compressed latent spaces inherently discards fine-grained structural details. In this paper, we propose a novel two-stage framework that adapts the generative prior of a few-step flow-matching backbone to real-world dehazing. In the first stage, we fine-tune the latent backbone using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), supervised not only on a flow-matching objective, but also on pixel-level supervision, thus enabling direct hazy-to-clear translation. In the second stage, we introduce structure-preserving skip connections directly to the VAE decoder, bypassing latent compression artifacts to recover precise spatial edges. Experiments on four realworld benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing dehazing methods in real conditions.

articles.title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
articles.summary: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.

articles.title: VidForce: Predicting Force-Aware Articulation by Observing Humans
articles.summary: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. Project page: https://rafaymhddn.github.io/vidforce

articles.title: CoReQ: Condition-Aware Cross-Modal Repair and Quality-Guided Robust Collaborative Perception
articles.summary: Multi-vehicle collaborative perception can use observations from different perspectives to alleviate the problems of occlusion and limited sensing range. However, missing echoes and false echoes caused by bad weather will reduce the quality of single-vehicle features and affect collaborative detection. LiDAR provides richer geometric information, and 4D Radar has strong weather adaptability. The complementarity of the two provides the possibility to improve perception under degraded observations. However, how to adjust cross-modal repair according to the current observation conditions and how to reasonably integrate multi-vehicle features whose reliability still differs after repair are still problems that need to be solved. To this end, we propose CoReQ, a condition-aware repair and quality-guided collaborative perception framework. For the former, the condition-guided bidirectional cross-modal repair module (CBCR) extracts vehicle-level observation conditions from point cloud occupancy, density and feature statistics, and adjusts the bidirectional correction of LiDAR and Radar features accordingly. For the latter, we combine local reliability assessment with collaborative weighting: first, the task-aware quality estimation module (TaQE) uses the classification and positioning information of the EMA teacher to construct a supervision target and predict the spatial quality of the repaired features; then, the condition and quality guided fusion module (CoQF) matches the quality information with the content, and the observation conditions of both parties are jointly used for multi-vehicle feature weighted fusion. Experiments on V2X-R and V2X-Radar-C show that the framework is competitive under a variety of observation conditions, achieving significant gains in AP@0.7 on V2X-R under snowy conditions, and achieving the highest AP among the compared V2X-Radar-C methods.

articles.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
articles.summary: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

articles.title: Modelling Billingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration
articles.summary: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.

articles.title: Transferable, Time-Parallel Graph Dynamics via Space-Time Factorization
articles.summary: Time-parallel neural operators (FNO and successors) have transformed PDE surrogates on regular grids. Mesh-based operators (MeshGraphNets, Transolver) extend operator learning to irregular geometries, but jointly learning across diverse topologies while retaining non-recurrent temporal evaluation remains challenging. We propose space-time factorization: partition the model into local temporal operators (learned, graph-independent) and a spatial mixer that propagates information across nodes without graph-dependent learned parameters. This structural condition lets the same parameters run on unseen graphs; non-recurrent instances also admit time-parallel evaluation. Accurate zero-shot transfer further depends on controlling three information leaks (graph-dependent weights, graph-specific features, and graph-correlated training distributions) and on suitable task physics and training coverage. The protocol applies to two distinct spatial-mixer families, fixed-spectral and learned-attention. We validate the principle in three domains. For floodwave propagation in river networks, a 27K-parameter model trained on the Yangtze transfers zero-shot to the Mississippi with median NSE 0.998 in boundary-conditioned operational evaluation, training 5.5x faster than a stabilized recurrent baseline. On cross-geometry Navier-Stokes, the three-seed SepFNO mean relative vorticity error on five unseen targets falls by about 28% from 5 to 12 training geometries, with a consistent single-run SepTransolver trend. On cross-city traffic forecasting, zero-shot transfer reaches within 12.9% of an oracle trained on the target city. Across settings, cross-geometry error decreases with both the number of training geometries and their relatedness to the test, at a rate depending on the spatial mixer. This opens the path to pooled-data, foundation-style models for graph dynamics on irregular topologies.

articles.title: Semidefinite Programming for Cold-Start GNSS Doppler-Based Alignment: A Comparison with Nonlinear Least Squares
articles.summary: Initial attitude alignment between local navigation frames and the Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF) frame is a critical prerequisite for multi-sensor integrated navigation, such as Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)/inertial/odometry fusion, before global and local measurements can be jointly processed. While GNSS Doppler-based alignment eliminates the need for carrier-phase ambiguity resolution or multi-antenna hardware, solving this non-convex problem via local nonlinear least squares (NLS) suffers from local minima, whereas direct semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation incurs high latency and omits local covariance outputs. This study systematically compares NLS and SDP on a unified maximum-likelihood Doppler objective across Monte Carlo simulations and three real-world driving datasets. We demonstrate that attaching a modular dual SDP certifier to a standard manifold NLS solver recovers the global accuracy of direct SDP within 0.001 degrees, reduces real-world 95th-percentile yaw errors from over 86 degrees down to 2.88 degrees to 4.70 degrees, and cuts median solve times by up to an order of magnitude while preserving native Jacobian covariances. We conclude that candidate-driven certification bridges local estimation and global optimization due to two structural advantages: (1) our theoretical comparison reveals that SDP relaxation enlarges the feasible region while preserving the lifted cost, allowing Lagrangian duality to verify whether a fixed NLS candidate attains the global lower bound without invoking a full SDP solver, and (2) the candidate-driven architecture acts as a non-intrusive module that plugs directly into existing navigation pipelines without replacing the local estimator, preserving native tangent-space covariance outputs and low typical latency.

articles.title: Grounding Language Models in Revealed Audience Behavior
articles.summary: Language models are increasingly used to simulate how an audience will respond to a headline or a post, and such simulators are validated against what people say. We validate them against what people do. We call a model grounded in revealed audience behavior when it is fine-tuned on records of what audiences actually clicked, liked or watched, and we ask not only whether asking a model falls short of grounding it, as prior work found, but why and where. Why: the gap is a property of the training signal, not mainly of model size or prompting. The same 8B model is right about half the time when asked which headline readers will click and 86.5% of the time when grounded in the clicks; the strongest prompting we tried only matches a text classifier; a grounded 0.6B model beats every prompted frontier model in our runs; and whether the clicks are fitted as counts or as shares makes no detectable difference in a pre-registered test. The asked 8B model also reproduces stated-preference cues, favoring question headlines that in fact lower clicks. Where: across four behaviors, grounding wins where the text carries the signal (short-video likes, +20 points on 200 pre-registered videos), only ties an asked model given the reader's history (news clicks), and nothing text-only gets far from chance on watch time. Code, adapters and run outputs will be released.

articles.title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space
articles.summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query. Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.

articles.title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models
articles.summary: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.

articles.title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
articles.summary: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.

articles.title: Assessing Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cyber-Physical Systems
articles.summary: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.

articles.title: Next-Manip: On-Demand Agent-Policy Collaboration for Robotic Manipulation
articles.summary: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack reliable fine-grained control and incur high inference cost, whereas learned policies provide efficient fine-grained execution but struggle beyond their learned skills. Although their complementary strengths suggest combining the two, doing so requires repeatedly deciding which executor should act as task demands change. Instead of relying on the agent for each decision, we present Next-Manip, an on-demand agent--policy collaboration framework that decouples executor allocation from costly agent inference. We propose an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC) that allocates control between the policy and the agent through a lightweight classifier of current execution demands. We further introduce Task Dynamics Context (TDC), which packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references to support both agent reasoning and executor allocation. Across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, Next-Manip achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing agent inference costs.

articles.title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
articles.summary: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

articles.title: Decision Models: An Introduction and Capability Evaluation
articles.summary: Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need decisions that software can act on. Decision models provide these outputs through explicit types for choices, binary judgments, and policy scores. We evaluate the accuracy, output validity, and request latency of eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites. StartLux Instant achieves 95.3% overall accuracy, returns valid outputs on all 1,000 cases, and has a median request latency of 0.084 s. It reaches 99.4% on classification and routing and selects the correct response on all 100 tool-selection cases. The highest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations is 97.1%. These results show how a typed decision service can support fast, programmatic decisions and why its suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.

articles.title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
articles.summary: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.

articles.title: GoldiBench: Right Tools, Wrong Amount -- Benchmarking Agents on Effect Judgement in Professional Editing
articles.summary: Real editing requests describe a look, not the steps to reach it, so an agent that serves them must judge how much of each tool the look takes. Existing benchmarks do not measure this: their tasks either state the tools and values, or leave the amount open and are scored by VLM judges that pass more than half of half- and triple-strength results. We introduce GoldiBench, a benchmark of 500 editing tasks in five professional applications (darktable, RawTherapee, GIMP, Inkscape, Blender), solvable by writing a program or by operating the GUI. Each task pairs a START image with a TARGET rendered from a hidden program, so the amount is fixed by a known target; the agent's edit is re-rendered and compared with TARGET, and the same task is posed with the tools and values, the tools only, or the goal only, separating operation from effect judgement. Across 25 open, GUI and closed models, agents operate well (99-100% with programs from 4B up when told the values) but fall off a cliff when they must judge the amount: given only the tools, the best model passes 19% of the tasks with programs and 33% through the GUI, and scale does not close the gap. Manuals barely help; the measured TARGET-START difference more than doubles the pass rate, but the same difference shown as an image does not for open models. Allowed four renders, agents almost always stop after the first; forced to compare, the strong models double their pass rate. Agents know the tools, but neither read nor check the amount.

articles.title: MIFLOW: Dynamic Recent-Behavior Priors for Reference-Calibrated Online Flow-Policy Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.

articles.title: Look Where Camouflage Breaks: Concealment-Guided Observation for Camouflaged Object Detection
articles.summary: A camouflaged object can blend into its surroundings at one scale and become distinguishable at another. Yet a region's apparent ambiguity gives limited guidance on which observation would resolve it. The challenge is to connect the form and scale of concealment to the evidence that a new view can reveal. We introduce CamoBreak, an active framework for camouflaged object detection guided by a Concealment Spectrum. From the image and current predictions, the spectrum measures regional resemblance and boundary ambiguity across comparison scales, distinguishing persistent concealment from separation emerging at finer or broader scales. These measurements guide crop selection from the already-captured image and recognition against global foreground and background references. An object-conditioned spatial preference then selects where local evidence should update the prediction and feature memory, retaining target corrections while suppressing background distractions. Accepted corrections reshape the next measurement, while predicted segmentation benefit determines whether to observe again. Experiments across encoder families and related segmentation tasks show consistent improvements. Targeted analyses support improved small-target recovery, multiple-object coverage, and selective evidence integration. Code will be released.

articles.title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence
articles.summary: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.

articles.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

articles.title: AnyPrune: Optimization-Free Pruning for Any Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Pipeline
articles.summary: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines reconstruct a scene from images in a single forward pass, representing it as real-time-renderable 3D Gaussians. However, the resulting representations contain far more Gaussians than are needed to render the scene faithfully, especially when there are many input views. This drastically increases memory and storage requirements. Existing pruning methods either require costly re-optimization, which defeats the purpose of a single forward pass, or rely on simple strategies that do not exploit all the available information. We present AnyPrune, a transformer-based, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. To remove unnecessary Gaussians, AnyPrune learns and exploits pipeline-specific redundancy patterns through a short single-GPU training on the frozen target feedforward pipeline. AnyPrune achieves better rendering quality than existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings and generalizes to unseen datasets, as shown through extensive experiments across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input view counts. It prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ on a consumer GPU, faster than every method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. It can also be combined with the pruning built into feedforward pipelines, pruning further at moderate ratios while preserving or improving rendering quality. Finally, it can even suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that retains most of the quality.

articles.title: A Fused Gaussian Process Bandit Framework for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
articles.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used to maximize expensive black-box functions when direct evaluation is costly. In many real-world applications, the high-fidelity objective can be approximated by a series of lower-fidelity models that provide partial but informative signals at substantially reduced cost. Multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) algorithms aim to strategically combine these information sources to achieve an optimal trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost. However, existing MFBO methods often oversimplify the complex dependencies between fidelity levels or rely on heuristic acquisition functions that lack theoretical performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we introduce a new formulation of the MFBO problem as a fused Gaussian Process bandit and develop a corresponding Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. Our approach accurately predicts the high-fidelity function by fusing multi-fidelity observations through an autoregressive Gaussian Process model and explicitly quantifies the uncertainty arising from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The proposed method also provides theoretical simple-regret guarantees, overcoming a key limitation of existing MFBO algorithms that lack provable performance bounds. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated via both theoretical analysis and empirical studies.

articles.title: PFedHASNet: A Personalized Federated Hybrid Analog-Spike Network for Multi-Subject Motor Imagery EEG Decoding
articles.summary: Motor imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) data are often collected and stored separately across subjects or institutions, and EEG acquisition and annotation remain costly. Training models solely on individual subject data limits the use of information from other subjects, whereas centralizing raw EEG recordings raises privacy and data governance concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw EEG data, providing a practical approach to leveraging information from multiple subjects. Accordingly, we propose PFedHASNet, a personalized federated hybrid analog-spike network for MI-EEG decoding. The shared encoder integrates continuous-valued temporal features, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) spike responses, and channel-wise log-variance statistics through learnable fusion weights. Client-private residual adapters and classifiers perform subject-specific feature refinement and personalized prediction, respectively. Experiments on held-out trials from participating subjects across four public MI-EEG datasets show that PFedHASNet achieves the highest mean client macro-F1 among 18 model configurations in cross-model comparisons, while maintaining competitive decoding performance with a compact client-side model in comparisons using the same backbone. Ablation studies further examine the contributions of hybrid representations and personalization components to decoding performance.

articles.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
articles.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

articles.title: SoccerNarrate: Event-Grounded Streaming Soccer Commentary with Macro-Window Preference Alignment
articles.summary: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. Recent streaming video-language models make low-latency full-match narration feasible, but they often favor general descriptions rather than professional, event-grounded soccer commentary. They may describe nearby actions while failing to mention key events such as goals, cards, substitutions, and offsides correctly and on time. In this paper, we present SoccerNarrate to bridge low-latency streaming narration with event-grounded professional soccer commentary across data, training, and evaluation. First, we construct SoccerNarrate-Data, a large-scale time-anchored dataset with word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration. Second, we perform macro-window preference alignment (MWPA), which aligns the model with complete event-level commentary semantics by comparing causal multi-step rollouts from the same streaming prefix while keeping second-level inference unchanged. We further use event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives to emphasize event semantics over commentary style. Third, we introduce SoccerNarrate-Eval, an event-centric benchmark based on temporally constrained event entailment. Full-match experiments show that SoccerNarrate improves event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines. Code and models are released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/SoccerNarrate.

articles.title: AVQ-Attention-2: Adaptive Vector-Quantized Attention with Exact Local Blocks and Linear-Cost Training
articles.summary: Attention costs $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ in the number of tokens. Vector-quantized attention reduces this to $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ by clustering the $N$ keys, attending to the $M$ codewords instead, and its adaptive form, AVQ-attention, concentrates codebook resolution where a query's attention mass actually falls. We present AVQ-Attention-2, a better design that merges it with exact local attention and attends to the mean of each cluster's keys rather than to a codeword. We show three improvements: consistently better quality at comparable cost; training that now also costs $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$; and an approximation accurate enough that the layer can be dropped into a pretrained transformer without fine-tuning. Across a variety of sequence lengths the result is competitive not merely with other approximate attention but with exact dense attention, running faster than FlashAttention at little to no loss in quality.

articles.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
articles.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.

articles.title: NOBODY Was There: Bridging the Human-VLM Gap in Unwarranted Person Attribution Bias
articles.summary: Describing an image requires not only recognizing what is visible but deciding what should be inferred. We investigate a systematic gap between humans and VLMs in their tendency to attribute visible actions or events to people who are not present in an image. We term this behavior unwarranted person attribution bias and find that, across 25 SOTA VLMs, captions of person-absent scenes mention a person four times as often as human-written captions of the same images. Through a preference study, we further show that both humans and VLMs prefer captions that avoid such attributions. Motivated by this, we introduce NOBODY, a preference dataset designed to bridge the gap between humans and VLMs in unwarranted person attribution. Through direct preference optimization (DPO), we align open VLMs on NOBODY and show that their agreement with human captions on person attribution reaches or exceeds inter-human agreement, whereas nine existing public preference datasets leave this behavior largely unchanged. Furthermore, we show that human judges preferred the aligned VLM captions significantly more than those of the baseline model. Alongside NOBODY, we release NOBODY-Bench, which evaluates VLMs for unwarranted person attribution bias and their alignment against human captions and preference. Project page: https://pmadinei.github.io/NOBODY/

articles.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming for Robot Foundation Models
articles.summary: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.

articles.title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
articles.summary: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs. On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

articles.title: A Morphological Approach to Inverse Lithography
articles.summary: Lithography is a critical step in the manufacturing of chips that works by projecting light through a patterned mask and subsequently focusing it onto a photosensitive layer on top of a wafer. The task of finding a mask that prints a desired pattern on the wafer is called inverse lithography technology (ILT). The design of the mask is complicated by the fact that it must satisfy a set of constraints in order to be manufacturable. In this paper we provide a mathematical characterization of these constraints. Next, we develop a scoring function that allows us to measure whether a given mask satisfies the manufacturing constraints and if not, how badly the constraints are violated. Since our scoring function is (sub-)differentiable it can be used as the regularizer in a gradient-based inverse problem solver. We show that the resulting MorphILT algorithm that we developed can generate manufacturable masks that have nearly the same print quality as the (unmanufacturable) masks obtained from unconstrained inverse lithography.

articles.title: SPAR: Self-Referenced World-Model Rewards for Physical Alignment in Video Generation
articles.summary: Generating videos with physically plausible dynamics remains challenging despite advances in visual quality. Latent world models offer predictive signals for evaluating physical plausibility, but higher agreement between predicted and observed features may reflect easier-to-predict scene content rather than more plausible dynamics. We propose \textbf{S}elf-Referenced \textbf{P}hysical \textbf{A}lignment \textbf{R}ewards (\textbf{SPAR}), a framework that uses world-model predictions for inference-time physical alignment. SPAR compares each video's prediction error with that of static clips constructed by repeating its own frames, providing a content-matched reference for evaluating generated dynamics. To account for the uneven spatial and temporal distribution of physical interactions, we introduce a unified \textbf{spatiotemporal reward refinement} strategy. \textbf{Spatial refinement} emphasizes localized prediction discrepancies, while \textbf{temporal refinement} moderates brief error peaks and supplements prediction errors with agreement between predicted and observed feature changes. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SPAR improves the physical plausibility of both \textbf{text-to-video generation} and \textbf{image-to-video continuation}, bringing generated dynamics into closer alignment with the physical regularities governing real-world events. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/spar-page/

articles.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
articles.summary: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.

articles.title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
articles.summary: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one.
