This work proposes an online monitoring framework to detect anomalies in object state representations. Thereby, a key challenge is creating a framework for anomaly detection without anomaly labels, which are usually unavailable for unknown anomalies. To address this issue, this work applies a self-supervised embedding method to translate object data into a latent representation space. For this, a JEPA-based self-supervised prediction task is constructed, allowing training without anomaly labels and the creation of rich object embeddings. The resulting expressive JEPA embeddings serve as input for established anomaly detection methods, in order to identify anomalies within object state representations. This framework is particularly useful for applications in real-world environments, where new or unknown anomalies may occur during operation for which there are no labels available. Experiments performed on the publicly available, real-world nuScenes dataset illustrate the framework's capabilities.

articles.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
articles.summary: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

articles.title: Feriji: A French-Zarma Parallel Corpus, Glossary & Translator
articles.summary: Machine translation (MT) is a rapidly expanding field that has experienced significant advancements in recent years with the development of models capable of translating multiple languages with remarkable accuracy. However, the representation of African languages in this field still needs to improve due to linguistic complexities and limited resources. This applies to the Zarma language, a dialect of Songhay (of the Nilo-Saharan language family) spoken by over 5 million people across Niger and neighboring countries \cite{lewis2016ethnologue}. This paper introduces Feriji, the first robust French-Zarma parallel corpus and glossary designed for MT. The corpus, containing 61,085 sentences in Zarma and 42,789 in French, and a glossary of 4,062 words represent a significant step in addressing the need for more resources for Zarma. We fine-tune three large language models on our dataset, obtaining a BLEU score of 30.06 on the best-performing model. We further evaluate the models on human judgments of fluency, comprehension, and readability and the importance and impact of the corpus and models. Our contributions help to bridge a significant language gap and promote an essential and overlooked indigenous African language.

articles.title: Below the Stopwatch: Checking the Performance Claims of Coding Agents in the Kernel
articles.summary: Coding agents open many pull requests (PRs) that claim to make software faster. Most such claims also give a reason, such as "cache the result" or "read the file once". A stopwatch can show that code got faster, but not that it got faster for the stated reason. We present Below, a pipeline that checks these reasons at the kernel level. From 1,343 runtime-performance PRs in the AIDev dataset, Below extracts the mechanism each PR claims and maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that must change if the claim is true. A build agent that never sees the claim rebuilds the code before and after each PR. Below then measures both versions with plain timing runs, hardware counters and LTTng kernel traces. Most claims are not measured: 57.3% of the PRs offer only reasoning or no evidence, and only 31.4% state an effect size. Of 82 analyzed PRs, 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change and 22 ran slower. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 PRs (20 in kernel-trace signals alone), and 42 PRs also changed their output. Kernel signals move about 1.7 times as often for a faster PR's claimed mechanism as for mechanisms it did not claim; the instruction count barely separates them (1.15 times).

articles.title: Bayesian Optimization in Sequence-to-Architecture Latent Space for Zero-Shot NAS
articles.summary: Zero-shot Neural Architecture Search removes the prohibitive cost of traditional NAS, but its search process is typically based on the evolutionary algorithm (EA); lacking an explicit model of the objective, it often resorts to a near-random search through mutation. Bayesian Optimization offers a principled alternative by modeling the objective and aggregating information across iterations, but scales poorly to the high-dimensional, discrete, graph-structured spaces of modern NAS, restricting its use to only small networks. In this paper, we bring Bayesian Optimization to zero-shot NAS for large-scale architectures by learning a latent space via a Variational Autoencoder trained to reconstruct a novel prefix encoding of architectures and propose a proxy scalarization that combines several zero-shot proxies into a single Bayesian Optimization objective. After only 10,000 iterations of the proposed search algorithm (8 hours on a single GPU), our method found a network architecture which under the given model parameter count constraints achieves state-of-the-art results on three separate tasks -- image classification, object detection and semantic segmentation.

articles.title: OP2GS: Feature-Free Gaussian Splatting with Dual Opacity for 3D Instance Segmentation
articles.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an explicit and efficient scene representation, but its primitives do not naturally expose object-level identity. Existing methods either learn contrastive per-Gaussian features that need post-hoc clustering, or supervise identity encodings with view-consistent 2D masks. We propose OP2GS, a lightweight object-aware Gaussian representation that augments each primitive with an explicit instance label and a dedicated instance opacity $\sigma^{*}$, which serves as an instance occupancy field for object-mask rendering. This dual-opacity formulation decouples visual appearance from instance occupancy, so that $\sigma^{*}$ can be learned and the instance labels can be corrected without touching the appearance parameters $\sigma$ and $c$. We learn $\sigma^{*}$ with an instance occupancy loss that follows the standard transmittance-based visibility of 3DGS. A discrete regrouping step then corrects the instance labels using multi-view mask consensus. Since no high-dimensional features are required, OP2GS can be plugged into existing 3DGS training pipelines and applied unchanged to frozen 3DGS assets. On the ScanNet++ validation set with the official class-agnostic protocol, OP2GS improves over OpenSplat3D, the strongest comparable baseline, with both SAM and EntitySeg masks; it is also best on Messy Rooms and, under the Gaga protocol, on Replica, while storing only one scalar and one integer per Gaussian. Code will be released.

articles.title: LimeTree: Linear-Memory Graph Neural Networks over Tree-Graphs for Resource-Efficient Language Modeling and Context Extrapolation
articles.summary: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 10.84 in 35.5 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.

articles.title: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models
articles.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can be efficiently customized by fine-tuning only a lightweight connector, but this fine-tuning stage also exposes them to backdoor attacks. To counteract this threat, existing defenses inspect the behavior or the attention of the released model. However, they mostly inspect the model with all visual tokens, implicitly assuming that the deployed model sees the same tokens, which rarely holds since visual-token compression is widely adopted to reduce inference cost. In this paper, we find that compression can hide a dormant backdoor attack from inspection and awaken it during deployment, as the redundant tokens regulate the strength of the trigger. Specifically, without compression, the trigger is diluted by the redundant tokens around it, whereas compression keeps the trigger for its high importance and discards its context, a phenomenon we term context stripping. Inspired by this finding, we propose StripWake, a compressor-agnostic backdoor attack whose trigger takes effect only under compression. StripWake (i) poisons each training image in four views (clean or triggered, with all or compressed tokens) and asks for the target only in the compressed triggered view, and (ii) aligns the attention on clean compressed views with a frozen benign teacher to preserve clean utility. Extensive experiments show that StripWake stays dormant with all visual tokens and reliably wakes up under compression while preserving clean utility, is far more robust to existing defenses than published backdoor attacks, and generalizes to different architectures, model sizes and compressors unseen in training.

articles.title: Towards Explainable Industrial Anomaly Detection via Knowledge-Guided Latent Reasoning
articles.summary: Industrial anomaly detection demands precise reasoning over fine-grained defect patterns. However, existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), pretrained on general-domain data, often struggle to capture category-specific anomalies, thereby limiting both detection accuracy and interpretability. To address these limitations, we propose Reason-IAD, a knowledge-guided dynamic latent reasoning framework for explainable industrial anomaly detection. Reason-IAD comprises two core components. First, a retrieval-augmented knowledge module incorporates category-specific textual descriptions into the model input, enabling context-aware reasoning over domain-specific defects. Second, an entropy-driven latent reasoning mechanism conducts iterative exploration within a compact latent space using optimizable latent think tokens, guided by an entropy-based reward that encourages confident and stable predictions. Furthermore, a dynamic visual injection strategy selectively incorporates the most informative image patches into the latent sequence, directing the reasoning process toward regions critical for anomaly detection. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Reason-IAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple tasks. The code will be publicly available at https://github.com/chenpeng052/Reason-IAD.

articles.title: SWE-Proof: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World Issues with Machine-Checked Proofs?
articles.summary: Ensuring the correctness of LLM-generated code is a core challenge for modern software engineering. Benchmarks for agentic code generation check correctness with held-out test suites, which are inherently incomplete and increasingly susceptible to memorization. Formal verification avoids both problems, but existing work covers only standalone tasks whose specifications are given as input, not real issues, which touch large repositories and state intent in vague natural language. We present BenchProofer, a pipeline that turns a coding task with a known correct patch into a formally verified one: it writes a specification for the new code, summarizes the existing functions that code calls with axioms, and admits an instance only after mechanical and adversarial gates agree. Applying it to SWE-bench Verified yields SWE-Proof, 500 real issues whose correctness is formally verified rather than tested, and it extends to SWE-bench Pro. Evaluating Claude Opus 4.8, we find that verification catches what tests miss: nearly a third of test-passing patches admit counterexamples, which a structured natural-language specification does not fix, while a correct formal one lifts resolution from 85% to 95%. Writing that specification is the hard part: an agent that must write its own gains nothing over an unaided baseline, and only 56% of those specifications pass our audit. The usual failure is faithfulness, where a specification constrains part of the required behavior and leaves the rest free. Specification quality also tracks the outcome, failing on 92% of unresolved instances against 51% of resolved ones, making faithful specification synthesis a concrete open problem. Code is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/BenchProofer.

articles.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
articles.summary: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

articles.title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?
articles.summary: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at https://github.com/fuji1655/PDC-Bench.

articles.title: ProSG: Learning Progressive Structural Guidance for 3D Human Pose Estimation
articles.summary: For 3D human pose estimation from detected 2D joint locations, depth ambiguity remains a fundamental challenge. Even when two connected joints are accurately localized in the image, their relative depth along the camera axis can remain uncertain. Existing methods progressively refine pose representations through successive stages, with early stages emphasizing local 2D skeletal geometry and joint relationships and deeper stages developing increasingly depth-related representations. However, early-stage structural cues remain overlooked despite their importance for subsequent 3D inference. Our findings reveal that reusing such information provides complementary geometric guidance, particularly improving joint position estimation along the camera-space depth axis. We propose ProSG, a progressive structural guidance framework that preserves and aggregates intermediate pose representations from preceding stages to guide subsequent 3D pose refinement. Specifically, Structure Guided Accumulation (SGA) maintains a pool of these representations and adaptively retrieves relevant information for each joint and frame, enabling deeper stages to revisit early structural cues. Structural Context Reorganization (SCR) further reorganizes intermediate representations before they enter the representation pool, using compact structural contextual tokens to facilitate the effective integration of structural information across stages. Extensive experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP demonstrate the effectiveness of ProSG, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

articles.title: A Matter of TASTE: Improving Coverage and Difficulty of Agent Benchmarks
articles.summary: As agent capabilities advance, existing benchmarks, such as $\tau^2$-Bench, are becoming increasingly saturated. Yet constructing new benchmark tasks remains complex, costly, and labor-intensive. Moreover, the standard approach, in which scenarios are first written in natural language and then mapped to tool sequences, captures only a narrow subset of the tool-use patterns agents exercise. In this paper, we address these problems by reversing the task construction process. We propose TASTE: Task Synthesis from Tool Sequence Evolution, an automatic method that generates challenging tasks with broader tool-use coverage. TASTE utilizes an Adaptive Contrastive $n$-gram model trained on LLM-judged validity signals. This enables sampling valid tool sequences that cover a vast range of tool combinations. TASTE then selects representative sequences from the pool via clustering, instantiates them into complete benchmark tasks, and refines them through iterative difficulty evolution. Using TASTE, we construct $\tau^c$-Bench, a challenging extension of the three domains of $\tau^2$-Bench. We evaluate $11$ agent/user LLM pairs and find that models nearly saturating $\tau^2$-Bench suffer severe performance drops on our tasks (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash falls from $0.82\!-\!0.94$ to $0.28\!-\!0.61$). Beyond increasing difficulty, our generated tasks more than double the number of unique tool combinations agents must execute. Our results suggest high scores on existing benchmarks often reflect saturation rather than robust task-solving ability. By automating the generation of difficult, high-coverage benchmarks, TASTE enables continuous, scalable evaluation of future agents.

articles.title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.

articles.title: Learnings and Pitfalls from AI-Assisted A/B Experimentation at Scale
articles.summary: A/B testing underpins product decisions by providing trustworthy, reproducible quantification of proposed changes' effects. Growing large language model (LLM) capabilities have motivated efforts to automate experimentation workflows. Yet LLMs are nondeterministic and prone to hallucination, properties that conflict with the trust experimentation systems must provide. Experiments are also operationally messy: diagnosing anomalies, debugging configurations, and conducting bespoke follow-up analyses require flexible reasoning and manual effort. These tasks let agents accelerate experimentation without replacing its deterministic statistical foundations. We report lessons from building and operating such an agent. Our central finding is that this tension is resolved not by making the model deterministic, but by bounding where its nondeterminism can reach; the model selects and sequences procedures, while deterministic code computes every quantity it reports. Three consequences surprised us: withholding information from the model improved its answers, demand concentrated on mundane retrieval rather than the autonomous decisions we anticipated, and the agent's eagerness to help threatened statistical validity.

articles.title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
articles.summary: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope combines shared multiscale pressure encoding, learned scale fusion and sensor-probability averaging, allowing measurement sets to change without retraining. Separate models evaluate unstart detection and new-onset prediction within a 0.5-s future interval. Seven Mach-2.9 runs, each with one annotated event, cover downstream throttling, throat regulation and splitter adjustment; three are held out with fixed weights and source-derived settings. Across three training seeds, full-sensor detection achieves run-wise mean window $F_1$ scores of 0.834--0.964. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces detection-score variation across sensor subsets in both splitter runs while retaining mean scores close to those of the full sets. Regional detection favors cowl and high-speed-channel measurements during splitter adjustment and compression-side measurements during downstream throttling, consistent with their respective pressure responses. Complete-record evaluation shows that configurations with comparable window scores can produce different alarm timing and persistence. These findings connect sensor count and regional coverage to pressure discrimination and sequential alarm behavior, providing experimental guidance for configuring inlet monitoring systems.

articles.title: Frequency-Structured Hamiltonian Neural Network for Multi-Timescale Dynamics
articles.summary: Learning coupled fast and slow dynamics accurately remains challenging for structure-preserving neural models. Hamiltonian Neural Networks preserve a learned Hamiltonian, but their neural parameterizations are susceptible to spectral bias, which favors slowly varying components and can leave fast oscillations poorly resolved. We introduce the Frequency-Structured Hamiltonian Neural Network (FS-HNN), which organizes Hamiltonian learning across temporal frequency scales. FS-HNN learns Hamiltonian components from frequency-filtered views of observed trajectories and combines them nonlinearly into a single scalar Hamiltonian. This enables the model to represent interactions across timescales while conserving the learned energy in continuous time. For PDEs, FS-HNN represents Hamiltonian components as neural functionals and learns a spatial operator, using orthogonal projection to conserve the learned energy. Experiments on ODE and PDE benchmarks spanning nonlinear oscillators, coupled lattices, shallow water flows, and dispersive waves show that FS-HNN improves long-horizon rollout accuracy over existing baselines, with accompanying gains in physical-energy fidelity.

articles.title: BARISTA: A Multi-Task Egocentric Benchmark for Compositional Visual Understanding
articles.summary: Scene understanding is central to general physical intelligence, and video is a primary modality for capturing both state and temporal dynamics of a scene. Yet understanding physical processes remains difficult, as models must combine object localization, hand-object interactions, relational parsing, temporal reasoning, and step-level procedural inference. Existing benchmarks usually evaluate these capabilities separately, limiting diagnosis of why models fail on procedural tasks. We introduce BARISTA, a densely annotated egocentric dataset and benchmark of 185 real-world coffee-preparation videos covering fully automatic, portafilter-based, and capsule-based workflows. BARISTA provides verified per-frame scene graphs linking persistent object identities to masks, tracks, boxes, attributes, typed relations, hand-object interactions, activities, and process steps. From these graphs, we derive zero-shot language-based tasks spanning phrase grounding, hand-object interaction recognition, referring, activity recognition, relation extraction, and temporal visual question answering. Experiments reveal strong variation across task families and no consistently dominant model family, positioning BARISTA as a challenging diagnostic benchmark for procedural video understanding. Code and dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ramblr/BARISTA.

articles.title: When Successful Collaboration Becomes an Attack Surface: Insider Memory Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
articles.summary: Recent Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) increasingly use shared memory to store and reuse successful collaboration records, enabling teams to improve across tasks. However, this memory introduces a new attack surface for malicious insiders. Unlike existing insider attacks that inject misleading information directly into the current collaboration, misinformation stored in shared memory can later appear as successful team experience and gain greater credibility and influence. We propose MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits this vulnerability using only normal participation privileges, without direct memory access. During an earlier task, the malicious agent embeds a target-specific payload while helping the team answer correctly, allowing the payload to be retained in a successful collaboration record. When retrieved for a later target task, this poisoned record can steer benign agents toward a designated wrong answer, further amplified by malicious triggering. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA substantially outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. These results reveal that shared memory intended to accumulate team experience can become a persistent channel for insider attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahnji0520/MIMPA-code.

articles.title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests
articles.summary: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.

articles.title: Speak or Stay Silent: Context-Aware Turn-Taking in Multi-Party Dialogue
articles.summary: Existing voice AI assistants treat every detected pause as an invitation to speak. This works in dyadic dialogue, but in multi-party settings, where an AI assistant participates alongside multiple speakers, pauses are abundant and ambiguous. An assistant that speaks on every pause becomes disruptive rather than useful. In this work, we formulate context-aware turn-taking: at every detected pause, given the full conversation context, our method decides whether the assistant should speak or stay silent. We introduce a benchmark of over 120K labeled conversations spanning three multi-party corpora. Evaluating eight recent large language models, we find that they consistently fail at context-aware turn-taking under zero-shot prompting. We then propose a supervised fine-tuning approach with reasoning traces, improving balanced accuracy by up to 23 percentage points. Our findings suggest that context-aware turn-taking is not an emergent capability; it must be explicitly trained.

articles.title: Characterizing Datasets to Anticipate Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Performance for Radiographic Pneumonia Detection
articles.summary: Deep learning models for pneumonia detection from chest radiographs exhibit degraded accuracy when applied across institutions, which motivates Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA). We observe that UDA performance depends on the properties of both the source and target datasets, and that performance gains are asymmetric with respect to dataset pairs. We investigate which structural properties of chest X-ray datasets are the most important predictors of UDA performance, and whether they can be measured before adaptation is attempted. Five chest radiograph datasets were characterized by the class separability of their features, obtained from one forward pass of a frozen DenseNet-121 and summarized by the Silhouette Score, with the Fisher Ratio as a supporting measure. All twenty directed source-target pairs were adapted with a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN), while direct transfer without adaptation was also evaluated. Seven published transferability estimators were computed on the same representation for comparison. We found that adaptation performance depended on both endpoints in opposite directions. More separable target datasets attained higher AUC scores ($r=0.934$, $p=0.042$), whereas more separable sources produced lower AUC scores ($r=-0.922$, $p=0.017$). The signed difference in separability tracked the signed difference in AUC between the two directions of a pair ($r=-0.932$, $p=0.017$) and identified the better direction in 10 of 10 pairs ($p=0.001$). The proposed descriptor was comparable to the best published estimators on target evaluation. Source and target datasets play opposite structural roles in adaptation: higher class separability makes a dataset easier as a test set but not as a training source. This framework can guide dataset selection for adaptation in low-resource settings without running full experiments.

articles.title: ConsistWorld: Evidence Routing for Consistent Multi-Agent World Models
articles.summary: Autoregressive video world models enable temporally coherent generation for a single observer. Extending them to multiple agents requires consistency across independently controlled views and temporal gaps under causal streaming. We present ConsistWorld, a multi-agent world model that generates camera-controlled video streams of a static scene from one shared image. We formulate consistency as routing evidence from committed multi-agent history and concurrently generated peer views to the tokens being generated. Pose Conditioned Memory Retrieval selects relevant historical observations from all agents, recovering evidence beyond the recent context window. Visibility-Gated Peer Sharing regulates current peer information according to estimated historical coverage and current-view overlap. Together, they determine which historical observations enter the context and where concurrent peer information contributes, supporting long-term recall and coordinated exploration. Both mechanisms use camera geometry and maintain a bounded active context for a fixed agent count and retrieval budget. Experiments on evidence sharing cases and video length and agent number generalizations show that ConsistWorld achieves a strong cross-time and cross-agent consistency while preserving competitive generation quality.

articles.title: LLM-ACES: Closed-Loop Discovery of Dynamical Systems with LLM-Guided Adaptive Search
articles.summary: Recovering governing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) from data is a central challenge in modeling dynamical systems across scientific domains. Existing approaches cast discovery as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming that the observed trajectories are sufficiently informative. However, dynamical systems evolve over large state spaces, and limited data can make multiple equations observationally indistinguishable, leading to identifiability gaps and the recovery of incorrect governing equations. To address this, we introduce LLM-ACES, or LLM-guided Active Closed-loop Equation Search, a closed-loop framework that jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. In LLM-ACES, a large language model (LLM) proposes operator priors that define constrained subspaces of the symbolic search space, within which candidate equations are fit to the observed data. The disagreement among these candidates guides the acquisition of informative trajectories, creating a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics. On 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, LLM-ACES achieves the lowest median NMSE, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while reaching the highest symbolic accuracy up to 70.8% on ODEBench and 69.5% on ODEBase across different LLM backbones. Our analysis further shows that LLM-ACES is sample-efficient, achieving better performance with less data. Under observation noise and sparse sampling, LLM-ACES keeps the lowest reconstruction error without inflating expression complexity, whereas baselines tend to add spurious terms that fit the data locally but obscure the governing relationships. Code: https://github.com/scientific-discovery/LLM-ACES

articles.title: Unbiased Approximate Vector-Jacobian Products for Efficient Backpropagation
articles.summary: In this work we introduce methods to reduce the computational and memory costs of training deep neural networks. Our approach consists in replacing exact vector-jacobian products by randomized, unbiased approximations thereof during backpropagation. We provide a theoretical analysis of the trade-off between the number of epochs needed to achieve a target precision and the cost reduction for each epoch. We then identify specific unbiased estimates of vector-jacobian products for which we establish desirable optimality properties of minimal variance under sparsity constraints. Finally we provide in-depth experiments on multi-layer perceptrons, BagNets and Visual Transfomers architectures. These validate our theoretical results, and confirm the potential of our proposed unbiased randomized backpropagation approach for reducing the cost of deep learning.

articles.title: AdaGEM: Granularity Adaptation and Geospatial Evidence Modulation for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Understanding
articles.summary: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details and extensive geographic coverage for Earth observation understanding. However, such imagery generates quadratically growing visual token sequences, where sparse task-critical evidence is easily overwhelmed by redundant and task-irrelevant tokens, leading to excessive computation and ineffective evidence preservation. Existing methods seek to balance computational efficiency and task effectiveness through selective multi-scale inspection or direct token pruning, yet often overlook task-dependent granularity requirements and struggle to distinguish sparse critical evidence from overwhelming visual redundancy. To address these challenges, we propose AdaGEM, a unified framework that jointly adapts visual granularity to task demands and modulates token selection to preserve essential geospatial evidence. Specifically, a Granularity Router predicts detail requirements and evidence scope from the query, then selects input resolution and token budget via a rule-based mapping. At the adapted granularity, a Geospatial Evidence Modulator selects complementary visual tokens to preserve critical evidence and spatial context while suppressing redundancy in homogeneous regions. Extensive experiments across diverse remote sensing benchmarks and multiple MLLM backbones demonstrate that AdaGEM consistently improves task performance over strong baselines and existing UHR methods while substantially reducing inference costs.

articles.title: FastBridge: Closing the Model-Based Realization Gap in Safety Filters on 3D Gaussian Splatting for Fast Quadrotor Flight
articles.summary: Fast quadrotor flight requires safe obstacle avoidance under tight onboard compute limits. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides a continuous, geometry-aware scene representation for perception-driven navigation, existing 3DGS safety filters use reduced-order models such as single- and double-integrators that ignore actuator limits and assume commanded accelerations are realized instantaneously. Building on an analytic collision cone barrier for 3DGS, we introduce a nonlinear, actuator-aware safety filter enforced through the full quadrotor dynamics. We derive a high-relative-degree collision cone exponential CBF (ECBF) and a backup CBF whose forward-simulated backup policy provides a certified admissible fallback whenever the QP is infeasible under input constraints. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS safety filter, our approach reduces trajectory jerk by 47% and runs 2.25 times faster. We demonstrate the ECBF in simulation and validate the backup CBF on hardware for real-time navigation in cluttered, perception-derived environments.

articles.title: Differential evolution with perturbation for continuous function optimization
articles.summary: This paper presents differential evolution with perturbation (DEP) for continuous function optimization. Differential evolution is a simple and efficient algorithm. Perturbation is the phenomenon that the motion by the contribution of the main force is disturbed by the influence subsidiary power. In order to show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, we compare it to existing algorithms by CEC2017 datasets.

articles.title: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
articles.summary: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al. 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working-memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable by the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features--directions that act like leading, spatially coherent finite-time Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions maximally amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a "Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical results. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens applied to both model classes. We also introduce a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.

articles.title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
articles.summary: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

articles.title: FAVLA: A Force-Adaptive Multi-Rate VLA Model for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
articles.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general robotic manipulation, but contact-rich tasks still require timely action refinement using force/torque feedback. Existing force-aware VLA models usually align all modalities to a single low operating frequency, which discards high-frequency contact cues that are important for reactive action correction. Additionally, they use static fusion, which cannot adaptively balance visual context and force feedback across manipulation processes. To mitigate these issues, we propose FAVLA, a force-adaptive multi-rate VLA model that explicitly separates low-frequency semantic reasoning from high-frequency force-conditioned action refinement. Specifically, FAVLA uses a low-rate VLM to encode visual-language-force context and predict near-future force statistics, while a high-rate action expert refines action chunks using the latest force observations. To decide when to update actions, we introduce a Force-Adaptive Multi-rate Inference (FAMI) mechanism, which schedules the action expert's inference rate from predicted future force variance, keeping low-rate reasoning in stable phases and increasing update frequency near contact transitions. To decide how to use force, we design a Force-Guided Dynamic Fusion (FGDF) module, which injects high-frequency force features into the action expert and dynamically balances visual-semantic and force cues across manipulation stages. Extensive real-robot experiments on high-precision and contact-rich tasks show that FAVLA outperforms force-aware VLA baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88.8% and lower peak contact forces. Zero-shot evaluations further demonstrate FAVLA's robustness to visual distribution shifts. Our project homepage is available at this website.

articles.title: Hierarchical Deep Research for Physically Grounded System-Level Materials Design
articles.summary: Designing multicomponent materials systems requires evidence on composition, interfaces, processing and deviceoperation that is scattered across the literature. Language-model research agents can collect this evidence, but their reports are seldom tested against physics. Here we show that Deep Tree of Research, a hierarchical multi-agent system built on locally deployable open-weight language models, ranks first among 47 agents in blinded evaluationacross 27 nanomaterials and device topics. Candidates from local agents outperform those from the best commercial systems on nine of ten first-principles simulation metrics across five design tasks. In a sensing case study, the agent nominated a fluorinated silver-nanoparticle/MXene architecture for the short-chain pollutant perfluoropentanoic acid; after an expert replaced the anchor with an amine, fabricated sensors respond selectively and reproduciblyintap water, consistent with interfacial calculations. Hierarchical research agents can therefore turn dispersed literatureinto experimentally testable materials hypotheses under human supervision.

articles.title: Robo-Harness K1: Harnessing Robot-Use Agents via Perception Augmentation
articles.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) understand manipulation scenes and instructions, yet as robot-use agents they struggle to turn 2D observations into the 3D relations that motion requires. We introduce Robo-Harness K1, a robot-use agent harness built on perception as tools. K1 offers region grounding, calibrated depth and geometry, persistent visual anchors, and projected grasp candidates as callable tools. The VLM calls them to measure the scene, chooses its next motion from the results, and measures again after it acts. On LIBERO-PRO, K1 raises Gemini 3.7 Flash from 16.7% to 71.7% and GPT-6 Astra from 63.3% to 93.3%, with the largest gains on spatial tasks. Without fine-tuning, the Gemini agent transfers to three RoboSuite arms, dual-arm RoboTwin tasks, and mobile manipulation in RoboCasa. In real-world experiments on a Piper arm, K1 completes eight of nine concluded trials across three tasks. Agentic post-training further distills a frontier model's traces into a compact agent: trained on 107 successful episodes, Qwen3.5-9B reaches 44.2% on new initial states and 13.9% on held-out task conditions, versus 30.2% and 0.0% for OpenVLA trained on the same episodes. Mixed training on traces from four environments raises held-out accuracy from 11.1% to 27.8% and RoboSuite success from 28.3% to 50.0%. These results support perceptual tool use for deploying and training robot-use agents.

articles.title: FlowSteer: Towards Agents Designing Agentic Workflows via Reinforced Progressive Canvas Editing
articles.summary: In recent years, agentic workflows have been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing workflow construction still faces key challenges, including human-dependent workflow construction, the lack of graph-level execution feedback, and the inability to repair errors in-loop during long-horizon construction. To address these challenges, we propose FlowSteer, a new paradigm of Agent Designing Agentic Workflows - a single agent itself end-to-end designs the workflow that a downstream executor runs. To support this paradigm, we introduce the Workflow Canvas, a novel executable graph-state environment that returns syntax-checked execution feedback for every atomic edit. Built on the canvas, we further propose Reinforced Progressive Canvas Editing, in which a lightweight policy agent issues one atomic edit per turn conditioned on real canvas feedback, and is trained end-to-end via reinforcement learning. Moreover, FlowSteer provides a plug-and-play framework that supports diverse operator libraries and interchangeable LLM backends. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that FlowSteer significantly outperforms baselines across various tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FlowSteer-9B2E.

articles.title: Binding Constraints in a Strategic Technology: An Industrial Vulnerability Index for the Foundation Model Industry
articles.summary: Industrial policy directed at artificial intelligence has become substantial. Public investment concentrates on compute, where private capacity expansion is already underway, and is largely absent from grid interconnection and generation. Whether that allocation accurately reflects the most binding constraint in production has not yet been systematically measured. This paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Industrial Vulnerability Index (AIIVI) as a framework for assessing potential production constraints in frontier AI. We construct a composite index of input vulnerability for the foundation model industry from fourteen concentration and sustainability parameters, aggregated by an O-Ring functional form in which capability is strongly influenced by the most constrained input. AIIVI should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of production constraints. Rather, it provides an index-based approximation derived from observable indicators and weighting assumptions designed to capture relative exposure to input vulnerabilities. Using this transparent and reproducible framework for estimating the relative vulnerability of frontier AI production to disruptions across key input dimensions, we also evaluate the index at 31 August 2026 for the nine developers at the capability frontier. We find values of 0.75 under AI-elicited weights and 0.62 under equal weights. The analysis identifies compute and energy as the principal drivers of input vulnerability. Marginal changes in these dimensions produce substantially larger variations in AIIVI than comparable changes in capital, talent, or data. We highlight three exposures that receive limited attention in existing assessment frameworks: the increasing reliance on external debt for data-centre financing, local opposition as a constraint on data-centre siting, and export controls targeting deployed AI models rather than hardware.

articles.title: MUSE: Multi-Tenant Model Serving With Seamless Model Updates
articles.summary: In binary classification systems, decision thresholds translate model scores into actions. Choosing suitable thresholds relies on the specific distribution of the underlying model scores but also on the specific business decisions of each client using that model. However, retraining models inevitably shifts score distributions, invalidating existing thresholds. In multi-tenant Score-as-a-Service environments, where decision boundaries reside in client-managed infrastructure, this creates a severe bottleneck: recalibration requires coordinating threshold updates across hundreds of clients, consuming excessive human hours and leading to model stagnation. We introduce MUSE, a model serving framework that enables seamless model updates by decoupling model scores from client decision boundaries. Designed for multi-tenancy, MUSE optimizes infrastructure re-use by sharing models via dynamic intent-based routing, combined with a two-level score transformation that maps model outputs to a stable, reference distribution. Deployed at scale by Feedzai, MUSE processes over 4 thousand events per second, and over 55 billion events in the last 12 months, across several dozens of tenants, while maintaining high-availability and low-latency guarantees. By reducing model lead time from weeks to minutes, MUSE promotes model resilience against shifting attacks, saving millions of dollars in fraud losses and operational costs.

articles.title: Computational Social Linguistics for Telugu Cultural Preservation: Novel Algorithms for Chandassu Metrical Pattern Recognition
articles.summary: This research presents a computational social science approach to preserving Telugu Chandassu, the metrical poetry tradition representing centuries of collective cultural intelligence. We develop the first comprehensive digital framework for analyzing Telugu prosodic patterns, bridging traditional community knowledge with modern computational methods. Our social computing approach involves collaborative dataset creation of 4,651 annotated padyams, validated linguistic patterns, and culturally informed algorithmic design. The framework includes AksharamTokenizer for prosody-aware tokenization, LaghuvuGuruvu Generator for classifying light and heavy syllables, and PadyaBhedam Checker for automated pattern recognition. Our algorithm achieves 91.73\% accuracy on the proposed Chandassu Score, with evaluation metrics reflecting traditional literary standards. This work demonstrates how computational social science can preserve endangered cultural knowledge systems while enabling new forms of collective intelligence around literary heritage. The methodology offers insights for community-centered approaches to cultural preservation, supporting broader initiatives in digital humanities and socially-aware computing systems.

articles.title: SparVAR: Exploring Sparsity in Visual AutoRegressive Modeling for Training-Free Acceleration
articles.summary: Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) modeling has garnered significant attention for its innovative next-scale prediction paradigm. However, mainstream VAR paradigms attend to all tokens across historical scales at each autoregressive step. As the next scale resolution grows, the computational complexity of attention increases quartically with resolution, causing substantial latency. Prior accelerations often skip high-resolution scales, which speeds up inference but discards high-frequency details and harms image quality. To address these problems, we present SparVAR, a training-free acceleration framework that exploits three properties of VAR attention: (i) strong attention sinks, (ii) cross-scale activation similarity, and (iii) pronounced locality. Specifically, we dynamically predict the sparse attention pattern of later high-resolution scales from a sparse decision scale, and construct scale self-similar sparse attention via an efficient index-mapping mechanism, enabling high-efficiency sparse attention computation at large scales. Furthermore, we propose cross-scale local sparse attention and implement an efficient block-wise sparse kernel, which achieves $\mathbf{> 5\times}$ faster forward speed than FlashAttention. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SparVAR can reduce the generation time of an 8B model producing $1024\times1024$ high-resolution images to the 1s, without skipping the last scales. Compared with the VAR baseline accelerated by FlashAttention, our method achieves a $\mathbf{1.57\times}$ speed-up while preserving almost all high-frequency details. When combined with existing scale-skipping strategies, SparVAR attains up to a $\mathbf{2.28\times}$ acceleration, while maintaining competitive visual generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/CAS-CLab/SparVAR

articles.title: AdapTS: Lightweight Teacher-Student Approach for Multi-Class and Continual Visual Anomaly Detection
articles.summary: Visual Anomaly Detection (VAD) is crucial for industrial inspection. However, most methods are designed for single-category models, and Teacher-Student (TS) approaches, despite their efficiency, have not been designed for the Continual scenario, where they need a replay buffer. To bridge this gap, we propose AdapTS, a unified TS framework for multi-class and continual settings, optimized for resource-constrained deployment. A single shared frozen backbone acts as teacher and student, and lightweight trainable adapters, selected at inference by a prototype-based task identification (99% accuracy), store the knowledge of each category without keeping past data. Training is enhanced via a segmentation-guided objective on synthetic Perlin noise. On MVTec AD, AdapTS-M improves I-ROC by 11 points over STFPM and needs 4.3 times less memory than Dinomaly, which is 4 points ahead. In the Continual scenario, AdapTS-M reaches the best pixel-level AP with only 0.1% forgetting and no replay buffer. AdapTS-S needs only 23 MB, and with a MobileNetV2 backbone AdapTS needs 6-7 MB while outperforming the edge-oriented STFPM on all metrics. AdapTS is thus a viable solution for resource-constrained deployment.

articles.title: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers
articles.summary: Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. We study the excess error rate of ECOC over the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier outputs a posterior estimate whose log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, we derive an upper bound from the union and Chernoff bounds and a lower bound from the nearest competing category and the Mills ratio. The bounds show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate. The excess error rate stays bounded away from zero, by a constant that depends on the two largest posteriors and the noise level but not on the number of categories $M$, whenever the distance between the code words of the two most probable categories is bounded; for equidistant codes this distance is $d_{\min}$. Conversely, it is at most $M-1$ times a factor that is exponentially small in the minimum distance $d_{\min}$, and it vanishes whenever $\kappa\,d_{\min}-\ln(M-1)\to\infty$ for an explicit $\kappa$ (for general codes, under a posterior condition). For $n$-vs-rest codes with $n\geq2$, the upper and lower exponents coincide asymptotically, which determines the reliability function of ECOC in closed form. The results extend to correlated Gaussian noise with the Hamming distance replaced by an effective distance; when noise is shared at the level of categories, the effective distance stays bounded and the excess error rate does not vanish for any code. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. In a semi-synthetic setting, the measured decay agrees with the predicted exponent. On ResNet-50 features of CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k, the excess error over a log-likelihood decoding reference decreases with $d_{\min}$ and, for larger $M$, levels off at a moderate distance, while codes with $d_{\min}=1$ degrade as $M$ grows.

articles.title: CryoGaussian: Heterogeneous Cryo-EM Reconstruction Made Explicit with Gaussian Splatting
articles.summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) determines macromolecular structures from noisy particle images. However, rare, transient compositional states and subtle, continuous conformational variation are difficult to resolve. We present CryoGaussian, a Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to the particle images through a differentiable rasterizer rendering orthographic line integrals modulated by the contrast transfer function. The Gaussians are initialized randomly, with their number derived from the estimated spatial support of the molecular density and their minimum size bounded by the Nyquist frequency of the particle images. To capture the compositional and conformational variation across particle images, we learn particle-image and per-Gaussian latents that jointly modulate the base position, amplitude, and scale of each Gaussian. Each structural state is then reconstructed by fitting the Gaussians conditioned on its inferred latent. On CryoBench, CryoGaussian achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for both compositional and conformational heterogeneity. On experimental data, it resolves a rare compositional state of the 50S ribosomal subunit (class C4, 1.3% of particles) with rRNA helix 68 docked in the absence of the central protuberance, and continuous conformational motion of the SF3b and helicase subcomplexes of the pre-catalytic spliceosome. We further optimize the rasterizer for additive cryo-EM projection, reducing training time by 12.8-28.0$\times$. Reconstructed density maps are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZiwenWang28/CryoGaussian.

articles.title: CrossProjection: Benchmarking Spatial Grounding across Projection and Section Views
articles.summary: Plans, elevations, and sections describe a three-dimensional structure through incomplete projections that change how an entity is drawn, not only where it is seen from. Reading them means deciding which entities correspond across views and recovering where they lie. We introduce CrossProjection, a benchmark that uses architectural drawings to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) can turn correspondence decisions into geometric answers. Its tasks cover cross-view matching, projection registration, and novel-section prediction, with outputs ranging from judgments and candidate selection to free region boxes and directed section cuts. For inverse section localization, we introduce, to our knowledge, the first VLM benchmark protocol that accepts any cut within an expert-adjudicated band of compatible positions and checks the viewing direction separately. Manually annotated drawings and BIM-derived views provide 33,788 questions from 46 buildings, and we evaluate 22 VLMs on a common set of 2,763. Strong selection or reproduction does not imply cross-view localization: on 100 matched region targets, the best model redraws 98 marked boxes but localizes only 59 across views. Section cuts remain far from expert level, with the leading model trailing two architects by 51.9 and 67.4 percentage points on shared Natural and BIM line questions. Incorrect choices favor mirrored positions, and many cuts face the correct way but violate local geometry. Curriculum fine-tuning on BIM supervision teaches a 9B model to localize regions it could not localize before, raising box accuracy from 0% to 25.3% on held-out BIM buildings and from 0.3% to 30.8% on real drawing sets not used for fine-tuning, whereas section cuts remain largely out of reach.

articles.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
articles.summary: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g. MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

articles.title: BEAVER: An Efficient Deterministic LLM Verifier
articles.summary: As large language models (LLMs) transition from research prototypes to production systems, practitioners need reliable ways to verify model outputs before they are deployed. While sampling-based estimates provide an ad-hoc intuition of model behavior, they offer no sound guarantees. We present BEAVER, the first practical framework for computing deterministic, sound bounds on the probability that an LLM's response to a prompt satisfies a property. Given a prompt and an oracle, BEAVER systematically explores the model's output distribution using a *token trie* and a *frontier*, maintaining provably sound bounds at every iteration. We formalize the LLM verification problem, prove that BEAVER's bounds are sound and that its selection strategy Max-$\mu$ is optimal for verification upto any tolerance. On 3 important safety tasks across 5 popular LLMs, BEAVER certifies up to $7.6\times$ more prompts as risky than a sampling-based verifier while using fewer forward passes, and its per-prompt bounds extend to statistical certificates over distributions of prompts.

articles.title: Repairing Reward Functions with Feedback to Mitigate Reward Hacking
articles.summary: Human-designed reward functions for reinforcement learning (RL) agents are frequently misaligned with the humans' true, unobservable objectives, and thus act only as proxies. Optimizing for a misspecified proxy reward function often induces reward hacking, resulting in a policy misaligned with the human's true objectives. An alternative is to perform RL from human feedback, which involves learning a reward function from scratch by collecting human preferences over pairs of trajectories. However, building such datasets is costly. To address the limitations of both approaches, we propose Preference-Based Reward Repair (PBRR): an automated iterative framework that repairs a human-specified proxy reward function by learning an additive, transition-dependent correction term from preferences. A manually specified reward function can yield policies that are highly suboptimal under the ground-truth objective, yet corrections on only a few transitions may suffice to recover optimal performance. To identify and correct for those transitions, PBRR uses a targeted exploration strategy and a new preference-learning objective. We prove in tabular domains PBRR has a cumulative regret that matches, up to constants, that of prior preference-based RL methods. In addition, on a suite of reward-hacking benchmarks, PBRR consistently outperforms baselines that learn a reward function from scratch from preferences or modify the proxy reward function using other approaches, requiring substantially fewer preferences to learn high performing policies.

articles.title: Patient-Zero: Scaling Synthetic Patient Agents to Real-World Distributions without Real Patient Data
articles.summary: Synthetic data generation with Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising solution in the medical domain to mitigate data scarcity and privacy constraints. However, existing approaches remain constrained by their derivative nature, relying on real-world records, which pose privacy risks and distribution biases. Furthermore, current patient agents face the Stability-Plasticity Dilemma, struggling to maintain clinical consistency during dynamic inquiries. To address these challenges, we introduce Patient-Zero, a novel framework for ab initio patient simulation that requires no real medical records. Our Medically-Aligned Hierarchical Synthesis framework generates comprehensive and diverse patient records from medical knowledge via stratified attribute permutation. To support rigorous clinical interaction, we design a Dual-Track Cognitive Memory System to enable agents dynamically update memory while preserving logical consistency and persona adherence. Extensive evaluations show that Patient-Zero outperforms baselines in both data quality and interaction fidelity. In physician evaluations, our records obtain the highest mean diversity, consistency, and completeness ratings. Downstream medical reasoning model trained on our synthetic dataset shows substantial performance gains (MedQA +24.0%; MMLU +14.5%), demonstrating the practical utility of our framework.

articles.title: SplatFlow3D: Learning Scene Flow via 3D Motion Feature Splatting
articles.summary: Considering the motion continuity and stability of 3D objects over short inter-frame intervals, introducing multi-frame settings in scene flow estimation can potentially address occlusion. In this paper, we propose a two-frame backbone, SimpleFlow3D, which integrates dense information from the image plane and sparse information from the depth dimension in a decoupling-followed-by-coupling manner by hierarchically constructing the 3D motion feature. SimpleFlow3D achieves SOTA results with minimal parameters. We also propose a weight-sharing multi-frame framework to splat the previous 3D motion feature to the current estimation process. The framework unifies the first and non-first frame inference by constructing pseudo inputs. After combining the proposed framework and backbone, the newly born multi-frame method SplatFlow3D further advances the state of the art. It achieves lower errors than the two-frame backbone, with fewer parameters than current methods. On both KITTI and Spring, SplatFlow3D ranked 1st over all published and submitted methods. Experiments show that SplatFlow3D improves occlusion handling, non-rigid motion estimation, and generalization to real-world scenes. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/SplatFlow3D.

articles.title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
articles.summary: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV (95% CI 59.0-73.9%), 69.3% for MSI (95% CI 51.9-76.5%) and 63.4%-81.2% for breast signatures. Cross-scanner prostate grade agreement rose from 42.5% to 92.7%. Under full scanner-HPV confounding during training, AUROC fell from 0.80 to 0.68 with original model features but only from 0.86 to 0.84 with tempering. Unlike post hoc feature calibration, tempering used only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site calibration. These findings support tempering to reduce scanner dependence of pathology foundation models.

articles.title: Energy as a Service-Level Objective: Transaction-Level Energy Attribution
articles.summary: Service engineers assess every change against functional requirements and qualities such as reliability, performance and availability. Energy is rarely part of this assessment. When consumption rises after a change, the team cannot tell whether the increase is worth investigating, worth accepting, or neither. A change to tracing, retries or a shared component can affect consumption far beyond the modified component. This thesis asks how energy objectives can become actionable engineering instruments rather than reporting metrics. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) answered a similar question for reliability with service-level indicators, objectives and response policies. We take SRE as the guiding research vision and study where the analogy holds for energy and where it breaks. An energy objective could, for example, bound the energy per successful transaction under stated workload conditions. The thesis connects three threads into one experimentally evaluated methodology. Useful-work semantics define what a successful transaction is. Energy attribution assigns shared and auxiliary consumption to transactions. Service-level engineering decisions act on the resulting energy objectives. Existing work covers attribution methods, measurement frameworks and sustainability objectives, mostly at component level and without a link to decisions. Our prior work on service-level energy modeling showed that the energy of auxiliary services is often overlooked and hard to measure. Planned experiments compare aggregate, request-normalized and useful-work-based indicators under controlled changes to observability configuration and injected failures. Whether transaction-level attribution is needed for these decisions, or whether service-level attribution with outcome counts is sufficient, is an open question the experiments are designed to answer.

articles.title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
articles.summary: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

articles.title: Copy, Predict, Code the Rest: Lossless Graph Compression with Decoder-Side Neighbor Prediction
articles.summary: We present a lossless compressor for directed graphs. It copies neighbors from an earlier row, predicts further targets from the part of the graph already decoded, and codes what remains. Its main coder, the candidate-bit coder (CB), proposes a bounded set of candidate targets, mixes their probabilities adaptively, and codes the leftover targets with a popularity-aware model. The encoder tries a fixed set of vertex orders and storage directions and keeps the smallest file that decodes exactly. On the benchmark graphs outside our development set, the selected files are smaller than the best recorded WebGraph and Zuckerli files and the best published HyperFast results. These savings have a cost. CB decodes much more slowly than the baselines and supports only sequential access. A faster companion coder, CG, is still slower than the baselines on large graphs. An indexed variant, CS-RA, gives smaller seekable files than the measured access baselines on nearly all tested graphs, but its cold queries are slow, and it fails on one development graph. We also explain what successful and failed predictions cost, and when copying a repeated row saves information.

articles.title: SkillBoost: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting
articles.summary: Enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions remains a central challenge in real-world applications. A promising solution is to treat skills as trainable states and optimize them in the same way as model parameters in neural network training. However, data-driven skill optimization is prone to overfitting to the limited trajectories collected from real environments. Overexploiting these trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved cases. This tension motivates a constrained search view of skill self-evolution, governed by an exploration--exploitation trade-off. We propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework that mitigates both risks: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration draws on prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound. Experiments across 23 model--benchmark configurations show that SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills.
